stages.name: Labour market and unemployment
stages.title: Labour market and unemployment
stages.sub: After this stage the student can build a labour market diagram and use it to explain five causes of unemployment.

steps.q: On a diagram with wage on the vertical axis and quantity of workers on the horizontal axis, what does the price on the vertical axis actually represent for a worker?
steps.right: The wage paid for their labour
steps.wrong: The number of hours they work
steps.hint: Price in a normal market is money paid per unit. What is paid per unit of labour?
steps.pre: So the vertical axis measures the

steps.q: Firms' demand for labour slopes down and workers' supply of labour slopes up, drawn on the same wage-rate axes. Where these two lines cross, what is true of the wage and quantity of workers there?
steps.right: The wage and quantity that clear the market
steps.wrong: The lowest wage firms are willing to pay
steps.hint: Think about what happens at the point where a demand line and a supply line cross in any market.

steps.q: If you drew firms' demand for labour and workers' supply of labour on the same axes, with wage up and quantity of workers along the bottom, what would you now have?
steps.right: A full picture of the labour market
steps.wrong: Just a picture of one firm's costs
steps.hint: You have both sides of the market on one pair of axes now.

steps.q: A coal mining town loses its main industry and those workers' skills and location do not match the new jobs being created elsewhere in the country. Will they slot straight into the new jobs?
steps.right: No, their skills or location do not match
steps.wrong: Yes, any job vacancy will do
steps.hint: Think about whether a miner can simply walk into a job needing very different skills, in a different place.

steps.q: Someone leaves one job on Friday and starts a new one in three weeks, having spent that time looking and interviewing. Are they unemployed for a long-term structural reason, or just while searching?
steps.right: Just while searching, for a short time
steps.hint: Their skills match fine; they just need time to find and start the next job.
steps.pre: This short spell while moving between jobs is

steps.q: A ski instructor is fully employed in winter but has no work in summer, then is rehired the following winter. Is this a permanent mismatch of skills, or something that repeats with the calendar?
steps.right: Something that repeats with the calendar
steps.hint: The job comes back every year at the same time, unlike a declining industry.

steps.q: In a recession, total spending in the economy falls sharply and firms sell less. What do firms tend to do with the number of workers they employ?
steps.right: Cut back the number of workers
steps.wrong: Keep hiring at the same rate
steps.hint: Think about your AD/AS framework: what happens to demand for goods in a downturn, and what firms need workers for.

steps.q: On your labour market diagram, a trade union or minimum wage law keeps the wage above the level where the demand and supply lines cross. At that higher wage, do firms want to hire as many workers as are offering to work?
steps.right: No, fewer than the number offering to work
steps.wrong: Yes, exactly the number offering to work
steps.hint: Above the crossing point, the demand line for workers is lower than the supply line of workers offering to work.
